{{Short description|Concept in algebraic geometry}}
In algebraic geometry, a '''toroidal embedding''' is an open embedding of algebraic varieties that locally looks like the embedding of the open torus into a [[toric variety]]. The notion was introduced by Mumford to prove the existence of [[semistable reduction|semistable reductions]] of algebraic varieties over one-dimensional bases.

== Definition ==
Let ''X'' be a [[normal variety]] over an algebraically closed field <math>\bar{k}</math> and <math>U \subset X</math> a smooth open subset. Then <math>U \hookrightarrow X</math> is called a '''toroidal embedding''' if for every [[closed point]] ''x'' of ''X'', there is an isomorphism of local <math>\bar{k}</math>-algebras:
:<math>\widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{X, x} \simeq \widehat{\mathcal{O}}_{X_{\sigma}, t}</math>
for some affine toric variety <math>X_{\sigma}</math> with a torus ''T'' and a point ''t'' such that the above isomorphism takes the ideal of <math>X - U</math> to that of <math>X_{\sigma} - T</math>. 

Let ''X'' be a [[normal variety]] over a field ''k''. An open embedding <math>U\hookrightarrow X</math> is said to a toroidal embedding if <math>U_{\bar{k}}\hookrightarrow X_{\bar{k}}</math> is a toroidal embedding.
